facts.title: Born From Acid-Proof Residue
facts.text: Iridium was discovered in 1803 by the English chemist Smithson Tennant, who dissolved crude platinum in aqua regia and studied the dark, insoluble powder left behind. From that residue he isolated two new elements at once: iridium and osmium. The find showed that the leftover sludge other chemists discarded actually hid brand-new metals.

facts.title: Named For The Rainbow
facts.text: Tennant named the element after Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because its salts come in a striking array of colors. Iridium compounds can appear yellow, blue, green, red, and deep purple depending on the oxidation state. The Latin root iris also gives us the colored part of the eye.

facts.title: The Densest Metal On Earth
facts.text: Iridium is the densest naturally occurring element, with a density of about 22.56 grams per cubic centimeter, edging out its neighbor osmium in most careful measurements. A cube of iridium just 30 centimeters on a side would weigh over 600 kilograms. This extreme density comes from its heavy atoms packed into a tight face-centered cubic lattice.

facts.title: Nearly Impossible To Corrode
facts.text: Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal known and resists attack by acids, including aqua regia, at ordinary temperatures. It does not react with air, water, or most acids even when heated, which is why it survives where other metals fail. Only molten salts and certain halogens at high temperature can slowly get to it.

facts.title: Fingerprint Of The Dinosaur Killer
facts.text: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter found a worldwide layer of clay, dated to 66 million years ago, that was unusually rich in iridium. Because iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, they argued a giant impact caused the mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs. The crater was later found at Chicxulub in Mexico, supporting their bold idea.

facts.title: Rarer Than Gold In The Crust
facts.text: Iridium is one of the least abundant elements in Earth's crust, present at only about 0.001 parts per million. Most of the planet's iridium sank into the molten iron core during Earth's formation because it bonds readily with iron. The iridium we mine today is recovered mainly as a byproduct of nickel and platinum refining in South Africa and Russia.

facts.title: Guardian Of The Old Kilogram
facts.text: From 1889 to 2019, the world's standard kilogram was a cylinder made of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, kept in a vault near Paris. Iridium was added for hardness and stability so the mass would barely change over a century. The standard meter bar of the same era used the identical platinum-iridium alloy.

facts.title: Tipping Fountain Pens And Spark Plugs
facts.text: Because it is so hard and wear-resistant, iridium has long been used to tip premium fountain pen nibs so they glide for decades without wearing down. The same toughness makes iridium ideal for the firing tips of high-performance spark plugs in cars. Its sky-high melting point of around 2,446 degrees Celsius lets it survive intense heat without deforming.

facts.title: A Catalyst For Modern Drugs
facts.text: Iridium complexes are powerful catalysts in the chemical industry, famously used in the Cativa process to make acetic acid efficiently from methanol. Chemists also prize iridium catalysts for adding hydrogen to molecules with precise control, helping build pharmaceuticals. These reactions often need only tiny amounts of the metal to transform huge quantities of material.

facts.title: Light For Screens And Medicine
facts.text: Iridium sits at the heart of many efficient OLED display materials, where iridium-based compounds emit bright, saturated light in phones and televisions. In hospitals, the radioactive isotope iridium-192 is a key source for brachytherapy, delivering targeted radiation to treat cancers from inside the body. The same isotope is widely used in industry to X-ray welds and pipelines for hidden flaws.
